# Variolation (inoculation with smallpox matter) (`variolation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by quarantine, probability_statistics
- Core idea: Variolation deliberately exposed people to smallpox. Survivors generally gained lasting protection, but the infection could be severe or fatal and could spread to others until the last scab fell. The Boston records of 1721 reported roughly two deaths per hundred inoculated people, against about fourteen per hundred recorded natural cases. The groups were not randomly assigned, so the comparison supports a lower risk without establishing its exact size. Vaccination later offered protection without giving the recipient smallpox.
- Pitfalls:
  - Not isolating the inoculated, who then start an epidemic among the unprotected
  - Deep cuts, large doses and weeks of bleeding and purging as 'preparation', which raised the death rate in early European practice
  - Assuming a mild case in one person predicts a mild infection in another
  - Calling it safe; it kills some people, which must be said beforehand
  - Confusing it with vaccination, which uses cowpox and cannot spread smallpox
- History: china: c. 1549 – first reliable mention (Wan Quan); widespread nasal insufflation by the 17th c.; stories of an 11th-century origin are legend; india: 18th c. – inoculation by travelling practitioners documented in Bengal (Holwell 1767); claims of great antiquity rest on weak evidence; africa: before 1700 – practised in parts of West and North Africa; c. 1706 the enslaved African Onesimus describes it to Cotton Mather in Boston; islamic: by c. 1700 – folk practice in the Ottoman lands; 1714 Timoni reports the practice from Constantinople; Pylarini publishes his account in 1715; europe: 1721 – Lady Mary Wortley Montagu has her daughter inoculated in London; 1760s Sutton's light method makes it routine; americas: 1721 – Boylston inoculates about 240 people in Boston: about 2 % die against 14 % of natural cases
- Read:
  - Zabdiel Boylston, An Historical Account of the Small-Pox Inoculated in New England (1726)
  - Arthur Boylston, The origins of inoculation, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine (2012)
  - Donald R. Hopkins, The Greatest Killer: Smallpox in History (2002)
